value.overview: The Ovenbird (Seiurus aurocapilla) is a chunky New World warbler that breeds mainly in mature forests of eastern and central North America. It is named for its distinctive domed, oven-shaped nest, which is built on the forest floor. Unlike many colorful warblers, it is mostly olive-brown above and heavily spotted below. Its ringing “teacher-teacher-teacher” song is often easier to hear than the secretive bird is to see.
value.classification: The Ovenbird belongs to the family Parulidae, the wood-warblers, in the order Passeriformes. It is the only living species in the genus Seiurus.
value.identification: This medium-sized warbler is about 14–15 centimeters long. Adults have an olive-green back, white underparts marked with dark spots, a bold white eye-ring, pinkish legs, and a rusty-orange crown bordered by black lines. The sexes look similar, although females may be slightly duller. It frequently walks rather than hops on the ground, flicking its tail as it searches through leaf litter. Its loud, repeated “teacher-teacher-teacher” song is a key identification feature on breeding grounds.
value.rangeHabitat: The Ovenbird breeds across much of eastern and central North America, especially in large tracts of mature deciduous or mixed forest with a well-developed leaf-litter layer. It winters mainly in the southeastern United States, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a regular migrant and winter resident, occurring on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes from lowlands to approximately 1,500 meters. It uses forest, woodland edges, shaded plantations, and other areas with dense ground cover.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Ovenbirds arrive in Costa Rica during autumn migration, generally from September into October, remain through the boreal winter, and pass northward again mainly from late March through early May. They do not normally breed in Costa Rica.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly from late spring through summer in North America. The female usually constructs a domed nest on the ground, often concealed among leaves, grasses, or low vegetation, with a side entrance and materials such as leaves, bark, grass, and hair. She commonly lays about four eggs. Both parents feed the young, which leave the nest after roughly eight days and continue developing under parental care for several weeks.
value.dietFeeding: Ovenbirds mainly eat insects and other small invertebrates found in leaf litter, including beetles, ants, caterpillars, flies, true bugs, spiders, and snails. They forage by walking slowly across the forest floor, turning over leaves and probing the soil with the bill. They may also consume worms, berries, and other fruits, especially during migration or on wintering grounds when animal prey is less available.
value.behavior: The species is generally solitary outside the breeding season and spends much of its time on the ground. It moves through shaded forest while bobbing its body and flicking its tail. Males defend breeding territories with a loud, repetitive song, while females may use injury-feigning displays to lure predators away from the nest. Ovenbirds are secretive but can be locally conspicuous when singing. During migration they may travel at night, sometimes along weather fronts.

conservation.populationTrend: Overall populations have been broadly stable or slightly increasing in long-term North American monitoring, although trends vary among regions and local populations.
